tagline.text: The mountain battlefield in Ilocos Sur where the Boy General made his last stand, and its trek

location.label: Location
location.text: Mountain area of Gregorio del Pilar (formerly Concepcion), Ilocos Sur, on the foothills of the Cordillera near Cervantes

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–May dry season (local climbers also recommend September–January for green scenery and cool weather)

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: 2 days and 1 night (a day hike is possible but demanding)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱3,000~6,000 (per person, based on a 2-day, 1-night trip from Manila including transport, registration, guide and meals)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Laoag International Airport (LAO) or Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL), then overland

children.text: Tirad Pass is the battlefield of the Philippine–American War where General Gregorio del Pilar, leading about 60 soldiers on December 2, 1899, held off about 600 American troops for a day. You follow an old Spanish trail up to a memorial shrine, camp there, and climb to Tirad Peak the next morning on this historical hike.

Tirad Pass is a narrow mountain trail above the town of Gregorio del Pilar in Ilocos Sur, on the western foothills of the Cordillera. Mount Tirad itself rises near Cervantes, and the figures differ by source: Wikipedia gives its elevation as about 1,154 m, while climbers' records say about 1,388 m. Either way, it is high, steep terrain: the Ilocos plains and the South China Sea spread out to the west, and ridge after ridge toward Abra and Benguet fills the east. In April 2022 a law was signed designating the area a protected landscape under the National Integrated Protected Areas System (NIPAS), so the nature and the historic site are now protected together.

The pass is famous for the Battle of Tirad Pass on December 2, 1899. So that President Emilio Aguinaldo, who was being chased by American forces during the Philippine–American War, could escape into the mountains, Brigadier General Gregorio del Pilar, then 24, blocked the narrowest point of the pass with about 60 picked soldiers. Facing them were about 600 men led by Major Peyton March, mostly from the 33rd Volunteer Infantry Regiment. The Filipinos built several lines of trenches and stone barricades along the ridge and near the summit and poured volley fire on the Americans climbing the zigzag trail, holding on for nearly a whole day. For this reason the battle is often called the Philippine Thermopylae, or the Battle Above the Clouds.

The battle turned when Januario Galut, a local villager, guided the Americans along a side trail. When the rear was broken in the afternoon, 52 of the 60 soldiers were killed, and General del Pilar was shot in the neck and died. American losses are reported as 2 to 3 dead and 9 wounded, depending on the source. His body is said to have lain unburied for three days before an American officer, Dennis Quinlan, buried it with local Igorot villagers and left a marker reading 'An Officer and a Gentleman.' That one day let Aguinaldo slip away through the mountains and reach Palanan the following September. Del Pilar's name was given to the Philippine Military Academy's Fort del Pilar, and in 1955 the town was renamed from Concepcion to Gregorio del Pilar.

Today Tirad Pass is a hiking destination that follows this history. From the town you take an old trail that Spanish-era forced labor (the polo y servicio system) paved with stones; on the way you pass a marker for the place where del Pilar fell and the Tirad Pass Shrine, which has an equestrian statue. The shrine has a campsite where many hikers spend the night and then climb toward the summit before dawn to see the sunrise and the sea of clouds. The trail is rough and remote, so this is not a mass-tourism spot; it suits travelers who are interested in history or have hiking experience. Most of the fees and times in this guide come from hikers' records of several years ago, so confirm them with the town's tourism officer before you leave.

This memorial shrine has an equestrian statue of General del Pilar. It opens to the west toward the Ilocos plains and the sea, and large camping huts let many hikers spend a night here. Near the shrine there are also a cave where the general is said to have slept the night before the battle and a marker for the spot where he fell.

This zigzag trail is paved with stones wide enough for horses to pass. Its hairpin-like bends let you feel why the American troops could not climb it in one push. Wet stones are slippery, so wear shoes with firm soles.

This is where the American sniper who is said to have shot del Pilar took position. It lies along the Lonely Trail and you pass it on the way down, where you can read the markers and get a sense of how the battle was laid out.

The summit is very small, with room for only about five people to sit. The last 150 m or so is a steep rocky section where you need your hands, and on clear days you can see Ilocos Sur, Abra and Benguet in all directions. When clouds move in, the view can be blocked for hours.

The shrine's campsite faces west, so the sky turns red toward the sea at dusk. The wind is cool, and at night you need real cold-weather clothing, not just a light jacket. Check camping permission and the camping spot with the town first.

This small mountain town is the starting point of the hike and keeps the story of the battle alive. The town's tourism officer helps with hike registration and finding a guide. Buy simple meals and supplies before you set out.

A national historical marker was installed at the battle site in 1952. During the Japanese occupation the Laurel government created a Tirad Pass Medal, said to be the only military medal that government issued.

blocks.title: Combining with Cervantes and Bessang Pass

children.text: Adding another day for Cervantes, on the other side of the mountain, and the Bessang Pass site completes a history trip through the Ilocos Sur highlands. There is also a traverse that crosses over toward Sagada, but the trail is rough and recommended only for experienced hikers.

items.title: 2-day, 1-night shrine camping route
items.subtitle: Day 1 to the shrine, day 2 to the summit and back down

children.text: Take a bus bound for Candon from Pasay or Cubao in Manila. Many hikers take an overnight bus, and the ride to Candon takes about
5–6 hours
Arrive in Candon and buy lunch, food, drinking water and fuel. The village has few supplies, so buy almost everything at this stage.
Take the jeepney from Candon to Gregorio del Pilar (about
according to past records). The regular service runs only once or twice a day, so if you miss it you must charter one.
Stop at the town office to register and arrange a guide. Depending on the source, registration is
per person and a guide is about
per group of five.
Climb the old Spanish trail to the shrine. According to sources the campsite is about 2 km away and it usually takes
around 2 hours
Pitch your tent at the shrine campsite and watch the sunset. It is best to eat dinner early and rest early.
On day 2, eat a light breakfast before dawn and set off for the summit along the Lonely Trail. With a light pack it takes about
4–5 hours
Take your summit photos and start down. The last rocky section may have no rope or handholds, so ask your guide about its condition.
Return to the town and head out to Candon by jeepney or a chartered vehicle. Plan the timing around your overnight bus to Manila.
A day hike is possible, but you leave the town before dawn and walk about
8 hours
with few rests, so do it only if you are confident in your fitness. It is not recommended in the slippery rainy season.

items.title: Half-day history route
items.subtitle: To the shrine only, without the summit

children.text: Meet your guide in the town and finish registration.
Walk the old Spanish trail and look at the battle markers one by one. The signs are written in English and Filipino.
See the equestrian statue and the battle information at the shrine, and rest. Enjoy the view to the west.
Come down the same way, eat at a restaurant in town, and head to Candon.
Turning back at the shrine instead of going to the summit means a lighter load and less risk.
Take a bus bound for Candon, Vigan or Laoag from Manila (Pasay or Cubao). The ride to Candon takes about
5–6 hours
, and many services run overnight.
The fare recorded in an older blog was about
. It now varies by company and seat, so check when you book.
Candon is the midway hub of southern Ilocos Sur. You transfer here for the mountain town.
Flying into Laoag International Airport makes the overland leg longer, but it is convenient if you combine the hike with a trip around northern Ilocos.

items.title: From Candon to Gregorio del Pilar

children.text: It takes about
2–3 hours
by mountain road from Candon to the town. The regular jeepney leaves around 1 p.m., and the service from the town to Candon leaves early in the morning. The fare in the past was about
If you miss the regular service you must charter a jeepney. According to past records it cost about
one way, so it is better to gather a group and split it.
The road is mostly paved, but some sections are rough and may be blocked by landslides in the rainy season.
You can approach from Baguio toward Cervantes, and it is said to take about
4 hours
by car.
If you plan a traverse that continues to Sagada, go only with an experienced guide.
In 2019 the DPWH built a new 1 km tourism road on the Cervantes side. Check its current condition locally.

The dry season from November to May is the best time to hike Tirad Pass. The trail is dry and the skies are clear, so the chance of a summit view is higher. But the midday sun is strong and there are long stretches without shade, so carry plenty of water.

Some local climbers also recommend September to January, when the grass is green and temperatures are lower. Right after the rainy season the trail is slippery and clouds often move in, so if the view is your priority, December to March within the dry season is a safe choice.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Cool and dry, with morning mist
The easiest time for both views and walking. Nights are chilly.
Start early in the morning and avoid moving during midday.
The trail is slippery and landslides can occur, so it is not recommended.

Before and after the hike, stay in Candon or a small lodging in the town. Lodging in the town is limited and may close in the off-season, so check by phone or message first. Candon has mid-range hotels and restaurants, so it is a good place to rest for a night on the day you arrive from Manila.

There are no shops on the mountain. Prepare water, snacks, rice and canned food in Candon and fill any gaps at the town's stores. Try Ilocos specialties such as empanada and bagnet in Candon and Vigan. Carry your trash back out to protect the shrine's environment.
Before you leave, contact the town's tourism officer in Gregorio del Pilar to confirm your guide, the registration procedure and camping permission.
Fill up on water in the town. Some records say there is water near the shrine, but that cannot be taken for granted, and there is no water on the shortcut trail.
Non-slip trekking shoes, rain gear, cold-weather clothing and a headlamp are essential. Gloves help on the summit rocks.
Phone signal comes and goes along the trail, so do not rely on it, and share your plan with the town office.
For a day hike, start before 4 a.m. and plan to be back in the town before dark.
At the shrine and markers, behave quietly in remembrance of those who died, and do not write graffiti or damage anything.
The last overnight buses back to Manila from Candon can leave early in the evening, so confirm the time.
The summit rock section is steep and slippery, and there have been fall accidents. If there is no rope or the cloud is thick, do not push on; turn back.
Avoid hiking in the rainy season, when landslides and river flooding are a risk.
Some sections have no shade, so there is a risk of heatstroke at midday. Bring plenty of water and a hat.
Some reviews report that the summit was closed, so check its current status with the town office before you set out.
Do not hike alone; always go with a guide.
Fees and schedules here mix records from several years ago, so give priority to the latest local information.
A UNESCO World Heritage city about
3–4 hours
away by car. It is a good place to rest for a day after the hike.
A UNESCO World Heritage church by the road in southern Ilocos Sur, which you can visit on the way up from Candon.
A mountain town reached over the ridge, famous for its caves and hanging coffins. The traverse is for experienced hikers only.
Another battlefield on the Cervantes side that commemorates a battle near the end of World War II. Visit it together if your schedule allows.
